title: Chapter 8 — General Survey Of The Subject
paragraphs: Before I close forever the theme that has held me so long, I would gladly take a parting survey of all the various characteristics of modern society and appreciate at last the general influence the principle of equality will exercise over the fate of mankind. But I am stopped by the difficulty of the task; in the presence of so great an object my sight is troubled, and my reason fails me. The society of the modern world that I have sought to describe, and that I seek to judge, has only just come into being. Time has not yet shaped it into its perfect form; the great revolution that has created it is not yet over, and amid the events of our time, it is almost impossible to tell what will pass away with the revolution itself and what will survive its close. The world now coming into existence is still half-encumbered by the remains of the world that is fading into decay; and amid the vast perplexity of human affairs, no one can say how much of ancient institutions and former manners will endure, or how much will vanish completely. Although the revolution taking place in the social condition, the laws, the opinions, and the feelings of men is still very far from finished, its results already admit of no comparison with anything the world has seen before. I go back from age to age to the remotest antiquity, but I find no parallel to what is happening before my eyes. Since the past has ceased to throw its light upon the future, the mind of man wanders in obscurity. Nevertheless, in the midst of a prospect so wide, so novel, and so confused, some of the more prominent features may already be discerned and pointed out. The good things and the evils of life are more equally distributed in the world; great wealth tends to disappear, and the number of small fortunes to grow; desires and gratifications multiply, but extraordinary prosperity and irremediable poverty are alike unknown. The sense of ambition is universal, but its scope is seldom vast. Each individual stands apart in solitary weakness, yet society at large is active, provident, and powerful; the performances of private persons are insignificant, those of the State immense. There is little energy of character, but manners are mild and laws humane. If there are few instances of exalted heroism or of the highest, brightest, and purest virtues, men's habits are regular, violence rare, and cruelty almost unknown. Human existence becomes longer, and property more secure; life is not adorned with brilliant trophies, but it is extremely easy and tranquil. Few pleasures are either very refined or very coarse, and highly polished manners are as rare as great brutality of taste. Neither men of great learning nor extremely ignorant communities are to be found; genius becomes rarer, information more widely diffused. The human mind is driven forward by the small efforts of all mankind combined, not by the strenuous activity of particular men. There is less perfection, but more abundance, in every product of the arts. The ties of race, rank, and country are loosened; the great bond of humanity is strengthened. If I try to find the most general and most prominent of all these characteristics, I will see that what is happening in men's fortunes shows itself in a thousand other forms. Almost all extremes are softened or blunted; everything most prominent is replaced by some middle term, at once less lofty and less low, less brilliant and less obscure, than what existed before.

When I survey this countless multitude of beings, shaped in one another's likeness, among whom nothing rises and nothing falls, the sight of such universal uniformity saddens and chills me, and I am tempted to regret the state of society that has ceased to be. When the world was full of men of great importance and extreme insignificance, of great wealth and extreme poverty, of great learning and extreme ignorance, I turned aside from the latter to fix my attention on the former alone, who gratified my sympathies. But I admit that this gratification arose from my own weakness: it is because I am unable to take in all that is around me at once that I am permitted to select and separate the objects of my preference from among so many others. Not so with that almighty and eternal Being whose gaze necessarily takes in the whole of creation, and who surveys both mankind and man distinctly though at the same moment. We may reasonably believe that it is not the singular prosperity of the few, but the greater well-being of all, which is most pleasing in the sight of the Creator and Preserver of men. What appears to me to be man's decline is, in His eyes, advancement; what afflicts me is acceptable to Him. A state of equality is perhaps less elevated, but it is more just; and its justice constitutes its greatness and its beauty. I would strive, then, to raise myself to this point of divine contemplation, and from there to view and judge the affairs of men.

No one on earth can yet affirm absolutely and in general that the new state of the world is better than the former one; but it is already easy to see that this state is different. Some vices and some virtues were so inherent in the constitution of an aristocratic nation, and are so contrary to the character of a modern people, that they can never be infused into it. Some good tendencies and some bad propensities unknown to the former are natural to the latter; some ideas present themselves spontaneously to the imagination of one that are utterly foreign to the mind of the other. They are like two distinct orders of human beings, each with its own merits and defects, its own advantages and its own evils. Care must therefore be taken not to judge the state of society now coming into being by notions drawn from a state of society that no longer exists; since these states differ so greatly in their structure, they cannot be submitted to a just or fair comparison. It would be scarcely more reasonable to demand of our contemporaries the particular virtues that originated in the social condition of their forefathers, since that social condition has itself fallen, and has dragged into one promiscuous ruin both the good and the evil that belonged to it.

But as yet these things are imperfectly understood. I find that many of my contemporaries undertake to make a certain selection from among the institutions, opinions, and ideas that originated in the aristocratic constitution of society as it was: a portion of these elements they would willingly relinquish, but they would keep the rest and transplant them into their new world. I fear such men are wasting their time and their strength in virtuous but unprofitable efforts. The task is not to retain the particular advantages that inequality of conditions bestows on mankind, but to secure the new benefits that equality may supply. We are not to seek to make ourselves like our forefathers, but to strive to work out the kind of greatness and happiness that is our own. For myself, who now look back from this extreme limit of my task, and see from afar, yet at a glance, the various objects that have attracted my closer attention along the way, I am full of apprehensions and of hopes. I perceive great dangers that it is possible to ward off — great evils that may be avoided or alleviated; and I cling more firmly to the belief that for democratic nations to be virtuous and prosperous, they need only to will it. I am aware that many of my contemporaries maintain that nations are never their own masters here below, and that they necessarily obey some insurmountable and unintelligent power arising from earlier events, from their race, or from the soil and climate of their country. Such doctrines are false and cowardly; such doctrines can never produce anything but feeble men and pusillanimous nations. Providence has not created mankind entirely independent nor entirely unfree. It is true that around every man a fatal circle is traced, beyond which he cannot pass; but within the wide verge of that circle he is powerful and free. As it is with man, so with communities. The nations of our time cannot prevent the conditions of men from becoming equal; but it depends on themselves whether the principle of equality will lead them to servitude or freedom, to knowledge or barbarism, to prosperity or to wretchedness.
